findings.summary: The tick makes ADR-0027's accepted false-empty reachable in production for the first time, and silently changes its quantity from bounded to unbounded. ADR-0027 (docs/internal/product/decisions/0027-one-refresh-attempt-is-the-accepted-bound-on-ambiguous-renew.md, 'The quantities' and 'Decision') accepts a KNOWN case in which renew() returns empty while this node has NOT been superseded: an ambiguous putIfMatch leaves a write queued inside the store, the next tick's one-attempt refreshed() (LeaseManager.java:296-301, 372-389) reads the pre-write lease and adopts its version, the queued write then lands and moves the version, and that tick's conditional write loses to this node's OWN bytes -- belief = null, empty returned (LeaseManager.java:319-324). LeaseManager's class javadoc names it explicitly ('Through `renew` it then stands down for EXACTLY the remainder of the TTL', LeaseManager.java:78-88), and the ADR is careful that the bound is the thing being accepted: 'The honest quantity is *exactly* the remainder of the TTL, unshortenable -- which is a materially different thing to accept than "up to"'. That bound holds only because acquireLocked() can take the lease again once it expires. This diff makes the empty set `fenced = true`, a volatile with no reset and no path back, and commitAll (LocalSequencer.java:241-249) then refuses unconditionally for the life of the object. Nothing re-runs LocalSequencer.start -- the class javadoc's own note says a supervisor tick is M5's, and DefaultIngest holds one Sequencer for its whole lifetime -- so the stand-down is no longer one TTL, it is the process's remaining lifetime. Before this change the same interleaving cost nothing at all through the sequencer, because nothing called renew(): the node kept committing into a chain no successor had sealed, which ADR-0002 classes as wasteful rather than incorrect (there is no successor in this scenario -- the lease on the store is this node's own late renew, unexpired). The path is not hypothetical; it is already pinned at the LeaseManager layer by LeaseManagerAmbiguityTest.aWriteThatLandsAfterTheRefreshReadStillSelfFencesOnce driving DelayedLandingStore. Neither ADR-0027, LeaseManager's javadoc, nor the backlog row is amended to say the quantity has moved, and the row's own stated aim is the opposite -- 'the outage this task removes rather than one it should add'.
findings.failure_scenario: A single renew's putIfMatch times out client-side while the write is still queued in the object store (the exact case ADR-0027 exists for). Tick N+1 refreshes, reads the stale version, the queued write lands, the CAS loses. renewForever sets fenced = true and exits. From that moment every bulk request to this pod fails: DefaultIngest.appendBatch -> sequencer.commit -> LocalSequencer.commitAll throws 'this sequencer lost its lease at epoch E and has been fenced', spending no store request but also never recovering. In M4 exactly one pod sequences (commit forwarding is M5, stated in this file's own javadoc), so cluster ingestion stops permanently until the pod is restarted -- where ADR-0027 costed the same event at one TTL of no sequencer followed by re-acquisition. close() cannot even hand the lease back, because renewLocked's fencing branch already set belief = null and releaseLocked returns at its null guard, so the successor also waits out the full TTL. Resolve by bounding the fence (re-acquire, or surface it so a supervisor can), or by staging an entry in baselines/review.txt that states the new quantity and amends ADR-0027's 'exactly the remainder of the TTL' -- the ADR itself says it is what should be reconsidered rather than papered over.

findings.summary: The WARNING asserts two things that are false in the one false-empty case the design already knows about. 'lost the lease at epoch E' and 'this node has been fenced' both claim a successor took the term, but in the ADR-0027 self-fence traced in M4.17-R1a nobody did: the object on the store is this node's own late renew, valid for a full TTL, and no other pod holds or can hold the lease until it expires. The comment above the branch states the same thing as fact ('Another node holds the term now, and it has sealed this chain'), which is true of the ordinary case and not of this one. Same defect class as the already-filed M4.36 -- a message that describes something that may not have happened.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator paged on 'lost the lease at epoch 7; this node has been fenced' goes looking for the pod that took over, finds none, finds the lease object still stamped with this pod's own id at epoch 7, and has no signal pointing at the actual cause (a store write that outlived its client timeout). The log line that fires is the only evidence the event produced, and it points away from the diagnosis.

findings.summary: close()'s comment gives a reason for not joining that is not the reason it is safe, and the reason it IS safe is undocumented and order-dependent. Safety does not come from 'the renewer holds no chain state'; it comes from two things the comment does not mention: (1) LeaseManager's BoundedLock serialises renewLocked against releaseLocked, so an in-flight renew cannot land after release's write -- release blocks in takeOrFail('release', ttl) until the renew completes; and (2) interrupt() precedes release(), so a renewer that has already passed its `if (closed)` check enters BoundedLock.takeOrFail with the interrupt flag set and gets an immediate IOException, rather than reaching renewLocked after release has set belief = null. The comment as written argues only that the ORDER of the two statements does not matter.
findings.failure_scenario: A later change reorders close() to `closed = true; leases.release(); renewer.interrupt();` -- which this comment's stated reasoning permits and which reads as tidier (release the lease, then tear down the worker). A renewer already past its closed check then reaches renewLocked with belief == null, renew() returns empty, and every graceful shutdown that catches the renewer awake logs WARNING 'lost the lease at epoch E; this node has been fenced and will not sequence again' -- a takeover reported where a shutdown happened, which is exactly the confusion the `fenced`-is-separate-from-`closed` javadoc at LocalSequencer.java:64-74 says the split exists to prevent. Nothing in the file or the tests would catch it.

findings.summary: close() now interrupts a thread that may be inside store.putIfMatch on the lease key, so the shutdown path can itself manufacture the ambiguous belief that release() then has to recover from -- the M4.35 shape, one class over. On a store whose I/O is interruptible the renew fails with ClosedByInterruptException, LeaseManager.renewLocked's catch sets belief = mine.uncertain() (LeaseManager.java:309-318), and the release that follows must pay refreshed()'s stat + get (2 extra requests, bounded per shutdown, so not a rate defect) before it can write the expired lease. The diff does not note that close() has acquired this hazard, and the interrupt buys only that the renewer exits up to one renew interval sooner -- a virtual thread that would otherwise wake, see `closed`, and return on its own.
findings.failure_scenario: SIGTERM arrives while the renewer is inside its conditional write. The interrupt aborts it, belief goes ambiguous, and release()'s refreshed() then issues stat + get against a store that is already the reason the write was slow. Either throws -> refreshed propagates -> release() throws -> close() throws -> the lease is not handed back and survives to its TTL, which is the ~10 s failover ADR-0007 and this method exist to avoid, caused by the shutdown path itself. Pre-change close() never contended with a renew at all, so a graceful shutdown could not create this state.

findings.summary: start() now acquires an unmanaged virtual thread that only close() releases, and it does so without changing any statement of that obligation -- start()'s javadoc (LocalSequencer.java:129-139) and Sequencer.close()'s contract are unchanged, and existing callers that deliberately abandon a LocalSequencer keep doing so. CommitProtocolSimulation is the one that matters: its zombie mechanism exists precisely to retain sequencers it never closes (CommitProtocolSimulation.java:100-107, 158-166), and each now carries a renewer parked on the PRODUCTION ticker -- Thread.sleep(RENEW) -- because tryStart uses the 4-arg start (CommitProtocolSimulation.java:244-252). That puts a wall-clock-driven writer inside a harness whose own javadoc says 'nothing here reads a wall clock or sleeps' and whose store's javadoc says single-threaded driving is REQUIRED because 'concurrency here would not corrupt the store, it would corrupt REPRODUCIBILITY' (FaultInjectingStore.java, class javadoc; its `injected` list and `drawCounts` map are unsynchronised). Both claims are now false, and neither was updated. Measured in the reviewer tree: 28 ms/seed at 120 rounds / 3 pods / ROUGH, against a 3000 ms first tick -- a 107x margin, so nothing fires today and the full :sequencer:test run emits no stray renewer log lines. The margin is the whole defence and nothing holds it.
findings.failure_scenario: One seed slower than 3 s -- a loaded CI box, a larger `rounds`, or M4.13's raise to 1,000 seeds, which the backlog row already owns -- lets a zombie's renewer call leases.renew() -> store.putIfMatch on the live FaultInjectingStore from a second thread mid-run. It consumes a draw from the seeded Random and appends to the unsynchronised `injected` ArrayList that the Result is built from, so theSameSeedReplaysExactlySoAFailureIsAPermanentRegression starts failing intermittently and, worse, a seed recorded as a named regression no longer replays -- which the simulation's javadoc calls taking 'the whole named-regression discipline with it'. Cheapest fix is for the simulation to inject a no-op ticker, which also removes the accumulating retention of every seed's MemoryBinStore by a sleeping thread.
